explanations.explanation: Envy is the one, friend. David says, "Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong." Fretting is stewing over what they're getting away with. Envy is wishing it were YOU getting away with it. David closes the door on both.

Close, because this psalm does get heated. But in this verse David never says to fight anybody. He says, "Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong." The second one is envy. Later he even tells you to refrain from anger, so the fists can stay in your pockets.

Fear is a natural pick when somebody's scheming. But David's word here is envy. He says, "Do not fret over those who do evil; do not envy those who do wrong." Envy is looking at what they have and wanting it for yourself, and that's the thing he says to drop.

Wither it is. David says, "For they wither quickly like grass and wilt like tender plants." Think of a lawn in a heatwave. It looked lush on Monday and looks like straw by the weekend. That's the picture he wants in your head when the wicked look like they're thriving.

I see why grass makes you think grow. Grass does that. But David says the evildoers "wither quickly like grass." He's talking about how fast it fades, not how fast it climbs. The next line adds that they "wilt like tender plants."

Spread sounds right if you're picturing a lawn taking over the yard. But David's point goes the other way. He says they "wither quickly like grass and wilt like tender plants." The word in the verse is wither, and it's the reason he says not to fret.
Yes, friend. David says, "Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart." Notice who gets the delight first. It's the LORD. The promise comes right after that.

Riches would be a nice line item, I'll admit. But David never mentions riches in this verse. He says, "Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart." That's the promise, word for word.

Victory sounds like a big, loud promise. But this verse doesn't mention enemies at all. David says, "Delight yourself in the LORD, and He will give you the desires of your heart." The focus stays on delighting in the LORD.

True. David says, "Commit your way to the LORD; trust in Him, and He will do it." You hand over your way, and the LORD is the one who does it. That takes the whole weight off your shoulders, which is good news for anybody who has ever tried to carry a full tray of cookies up a staircase.

This one is true, friend. David says, "Commit your way to the LORD; trust in Him, and He will do it." So the verse makes the promise outright. It's easy to hear a promise that big and look for the catch, but the verse doesn't add one.

Harm, that's it. David says, "Refrain from anger and abandon wrath; do not fret," and then he tells you where it leads: it can only bring harm. Fretting doesn't fix the problem. It just gives you a second problem, and the second one has your name on it.

Peace is what we all want out of a good stew of worry, but David says the opposite. He says fretting "can only bring harm." So the anger and the fretting don't lead to peace. David wants you to put them down.

Justice does show up in this psalm, but not here. David says that anger and fretting "can only bring harm." He never says they bring justice. Elsewhere, he says the LORD brings forth your justice like the noonday sun (Psalm 37:6).

David actually says the opposite, friend. He says, "Yet a little while, and the wicked will be no more; though you look for them, they will not be found." So you can go looking and come up empty. Nobody's hanging around the corner waiting for you to find them.

That's right, it's false. David says, "Yet a little while, and the wicked will be no more; though you look for them, they will not be found." You can search all you want and they won't turn up. That's the whole comfort of the verse.

The meek, yes. David says, "But the meek will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity." That's a plot twist, because the meek are rarely the ones who get picked first. The land goes to them anyway.
The mighty seems like the safe bet. They've got the muscle. But David says, "the meek will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity." The meek, not the mighty.

I get it, wealthy sounds like the group that's already got the prosperity. But David says, "the meek will inherit the land and delight in abundant prosperity." So the prosperity goes to the meek. Nobody in this line gets it because of a fat wallet.

Laughs, friend. David says, "but the Lord laughs, seeing that their day is coming." The wicked are gnashing their teeth, and the Lord is seeing that their day is coming. That tells us how this one ends.

Weeping is a tender guess, but this verse says something else. David says, "but the Lord laughs, seeing that their day is coming." The reason is right there in the verse. He sees that their day is coming.

Trembling would make sense if the wicked were in charge. But David says the Lord is not shaking at all. He says, "but the Lord laughs, seeing that their day is coming." The wicked are the ones who've got a day coming.
Yes. David says, "But their swords will pierce their own hearts, and their bows will be broken." The wicked drew those swords to bring down the poor and needy. The plan turns around on them.

That's a quiet ending, but it's not the one David gives. He says, "But their swords will pierce their own hearts, and their bows will be broken." The swords don't just sit around, and neither do the bows. This is a heavy part of the psalm, but the verse is clear.

explanations.answer: They are taken by the king
explanations.explanation: A king stepping in would be a tidy ending, but this verse doesn't mention one. David says, "But their swords will pierce their own hearts, and their bows will be broken." I think the verse wants you to see how the wicked's own plans come back on them.

True. David says, "Better is the little of the righteous than the abundance of many who are wicked." A small pile that's honest beats a huge pile that isn't. David has done the math and he's not worried.

It's actually true, friend. David says, "Better is the little of the righteous than the abundance of many who are wicked." Yes, the little of the righteous comes out ahead. Funny how the smaller number wins this one.

Forever, friend. David says, "The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance will last forever." He knows every one of their days, and the inheritance outlasts them all. That's a long time, even for a cookie jar.

A lifetime is a long stretch, but David goes further. He says, "The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance will last forever." Their days are known to the LORD, and the inheritance doesn't run out when the days do.

A generation is a decent stretch, but it's not what David says. He says, "The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their inheritance will last forever." Forever is the word in the verse. It beats a generation by a mile.
Smoke, that's the one. David says, "They will vanish; like smoke they will fade away." You can see it one second and then it's gone. That's how David describes the end of the LORD's enemies.
Stone is solid, and that's the opposite of what David describes here. He says, "They will vanish; like smoke they will fade away." Stone stays put, but smoke doesn't. The verse picks smoke.
Iron sounds tough, and tough things last. But David says, "They will vanish; like smoke they will fade away." Iron doesn't fade. Smoke does, and that's the picture he picks.

David says the reverse, friend. He says, "The steps of a man are ordered by the LORD who takes delight in his journey." So the LORD orders the steps and takes delight in the journey. He's not looking away.

False is right. David says, "The steps of a man are ordered by the LORD who takes delight in his journey." The LORD orders the man's steps, and He takes delight in the journey, too. It's a warm picture.

explanations.answer: The LORD is holding his hand
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. David says, "Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed, for the LORD is holding his hand." Notice that David says "though he falls." He doesn't pretend the man never goes down. It's the LORD's hold that keeps the fall from overwhelming him.

explanations.answer: He always lands on his feet
explanations.explanation: Landing on your feet would be a neat trick, but David says nothing like that. He says the man does fall, and the reason he isn't overwhelmed is this: "for the LORD is holding his hand." The credit goes to the LORD's grip, not the man's balance.

Good friends are a blessing, but this verse doesn't mention them. David says, "Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed, for the LORD is holding his hand." The reason is the LORD, and He's the one holding on.

Yes, friend. David says, "They are ever generous and quick to lend, and their children are a blessing." The righteous are generous, and their children are called a blessing. I think David wants you to see a whole household in that line.

That's a big job for the little ones, but David doesn't say it. He says, "They are ever generous and quick to lend, and their children are a blessing." The word is blessing. Rulers aren't in the verse.
Leaving the land would cut against the whole psalm, friend. David keeps saying the righteous will inherit the land. About their children, he says, "their children are a blessing."
Justice, friend. David says, "For the LORD loves justice and will not forsake His saints." That's the reason to turn from evil and do good. The LORD loves justice, and He won't forsake His saints.
Strength is a big word in this psalm's neighborhood, but it's not what David names here. He says, "For the LORD loves justice and will not forsake His saints." What the LORD loves is justice.

Sacrifice is a reasonable guess, but this verse goes another way. David says, "For the LORD loves justice and will not forsake His saints." The thing named is justice, and the promise tied to it is that He won't forsake His saints.

Wisdom, friend. David says, "The mouth of the righteous man utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice." What comes out of his mouth is wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice. Just try that at your next family gathering.

Complaints are easy to come by, especially when you're watching the wicked do well. But David says the righteous man's mouth "utters wisdom." His tongue speaks justice, too. Fretting is what David told us to drop.
Riddles would make a fun dinner guest. But David says the righteous man's mouth "utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice." He speaks plainly and well. No riddles are in the verse.
True. David says, "The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not falter." The law is in his heart, not just on a shelf. And right after that, David says his steps don't falter.
It's true, friend. David says, "The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not falter." The law sits in the heart of the righteous man. It's right there in the verse.

David says the opposite, friend. He says the wicked lie in wait, but "the LORD will not leave them in their power or let them be condemned under judgment." The LORD does not leave the righteous in the hands of those who are lying in wait.

False is right. David says, "the LORD will not leave them in their power or let them be condemned under judgment." The wicked may lie in wait, but they don't get the last word. The righteous are not left in their power.

explanations.answer: He passed away and was no more
explanations.explanation: That's it. David says, "yet he passed away and was no more; though I searched, he could not be found." That tree looked like it was going to stand forever, and then it was gone. David even says he went looking, and he found nothing.

explanations.answer: He turned from his wicked ways
explanations.explanation: That would be a happy turn of events, but David doesn't say it. He says the man "passed away and was no more; though I searched, he could not be found." The verse is about how he disappeared. A change of heart isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: He grew richer than ever before
explanations.explanation: That's how the man looked, friend. David says he was flourishing like a well-rooted native tree. But the very next verse turns it around: "yet he passed away and was no more." So he didn't keep growing.

David says something much kinder, friend. He says, "Consider the blameless and observe the upright, for posterity awaits the man of peace." Posterity means those who come after him, and they await the man of peace. Hardship isn't what the verse says awaits him.

False is right. David says, "Consider the blameless and observe the upright, for posterity awaits the man of peace." It's posterity that awaits him, not hardship. David wants you looking at the man of peace.

Stronghold, friend. David says, "The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; He is their stronghold in time of trouble." A stronghold is a place you run to when trouble comes. David says the LORD is that place.
Judge is not the word David picks here. He says, "The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; He is their stronghold in time of trouble." In time of trouble, the LORD is their stronghold.

Reward sounds like a nice thing to call Him, but that's not what David says. He says, "He is their stronghold in time of trouble." The LORD is their stronghold, the one they can run to when trouble shows up.

explanations.answer: Because they take refuge in Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. David ends the psalm with, "The LORD helps and delivers them; He rescues and saves them from the wicked, because they take refuge in Him." The reason is right there at the end. They take refuge in Him.
Offerings are a good thing, but they aren't the reason in this verse. David says the LORD rescues and saves them "because they take refuge in Him." It's about where they run when trouble comes.

Numbers don't come into this verse at all, friend. David says the LORD rescues and saves them "because they take refuge in Him." The reason is the refuge they take in Him, not how many of them there are.
